content:
We used to deploy the entire subscription in one go. The network, shared services, and workloads all went through the same Bicep entrypoint. It was straightforward to follow: one deployment described the environment.
That became harder to maintain as the templates grew. We were using Azure Verified Modules (AVM), and combining those modules in a subscription-wide deployment brought us up against ARM’s 4 MB template limit. The Bicep files could look manageable while the compiled template included the definitions of all those modules.
There was also the repeated work. Changing a workload meant submitting the whole environment again, including the network it depended on. Splitting the deployment into smaller stacks gave us a way to update those parts separately.
The next question was how to keep them connected. A workload still needs its subnet ID, even when the network belongs to another stack. I like to let Bicep read that value from the network stack, with the option to supply a subnet ID directly when using a different network.
We’ll pass deployment outputs, such as resource IDs and names, between stacks.
What is a deployment stack? An Azure deployment stack is a resource of type Microsoft.Resources/deploymentStacks. You supply a Bicep or ARM template, and the stack tracks the resources it manages.
When you update a stack, actionOnUnmanage determines what happens to resources that are no longer in the template:
detachAll: leave the resources in place, but stop managing them through the stack. deleteResources: delete resources that are no longer managed. deleteAll: also delete resource groups that are no longer managed. You can also use deny settings to restrict updates or deletions outside the stack. ARM still handles the deployment itself.
ARM limits still apply to stacks. Deployment-time savings depend on how you split the infrastructure and whether your pipeline skips components that haven’t changed.
Split by lifecycle For a platform with several workloads, you could use these boundaries:
Stack Manages Changes when Network VNet and subnets Network configuration changes Shared services Shared platform resources A platform service changes Workload Resources for one application That application’s infrastructure changes Deploy each stack through its own entrypoint. You can use Bicep modules within those entrypoints, but a main template with many local modules still produces one deployment request containing the module templates. Reading the subnet ID from an existing stack keeps the network deployment out of the workload template.
One resource group per stack I use a dedicated resource group as the lifecycle boundary for each stack. When I retire a workload, I want to remove its resource group and everything inside it as well.
There is an important Azure scope distinction here: a resource-group-scoped stack doesn’t manage its own containing resource group. Deleting that stack, even with deleteAll, won’t automatically delete the containing group. To include the resource group in stack cleanup, the stack must be created at subscription scope and declare the resource group in its template, with the workload deployed into it through a module. With deleteAll, removing that stack also deletes the managed resource group and its contents.
Deleting a resource group also removes resources inside it that the stack doesn’t track. That’s why I keep the group dedicated to that stack and don’t put unrelated resources there.
The output-sharing example below uses resource-group-scoped stacks to keep the Bicep files small. Each has its own resource group, but those groups are created separately and won’t be deleted when the stacks are removed.
Example: passing a subnet ID This example uses two resource-group-scoped stacks in the same subscription, each in its own resource group. The network stack in rg-network-demo manages a VNet and subnet. The workload-demo stack in rg-workload-demo manages a network interface that uses that subnet.
You’ll need a recent Azure CLI with az stack and Bicep support, both resource groups already created in the same region, and a signed-in identity with the necessary deployment, stack, and resource permissions. Reading outputs also requires read access to the source stack. The example uses Azure public cloud.
1. Publish an output from the network stack Save this as network.bicep:
targetScope = 'resourceGroup' param location string = resourceGroup().location resource vnet 'Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks@2024-05-01' = { name: 'vnet-platform' location: location properties: { addressSpace: { addressPrefixes: [ '10.20.0.0/16' ] } subnets: [ { name: 'workloads' properties: { addressPrefix: '10.20.1.0/24' } } ] } } output subnetId string = '${vnet.id}/subnets/workloads' Deploy the network stack:
az stack group create \ --name network \ --resource-group rg-network-demo \ --template-file network.bicep \ --action-on-unmanage detachAll \ --deny-settings-mode none In this example, detachAll prevents a resource from being deleted just because you removed it from the template. It doesn’t protect resources that remain in the template from being changed. none disables stack deny protection. Review both settings before using this approach in production.
2. Read the network stack or supply a subnet ID The stack stores its deployment outputs. In the workload template, declare the network stack as an existing resource. I use @nullIfNotFound() so a missing stack evaluates to null, and safe access lets the template handle that result.
The optional subnetId parameter takes precedence. If it’s omitted, Bicep reads the stack’s output. This keeps the same workload template usable with either a stack-managed network or a subnet supplied by the caller, without a separate REST call or output-passing script.
Save this as workload.bicep:
targetScope = 'resourceGroup' param location string = resourceGroup().location param networkResourceGroupName string = 'rg-network-demo' param networkStackName string = 'network' param subnetId string? @nullIfNotFound() resource networkStack 'Microsoft.Resources/deploymentStacks@2024-03-01' existing = { name: networkStackName scope: resourceGroup(networkResourceGroupName) } var resolvedSubnetId = subnetId ?? networkStack.?properties.?outputs.?subnetId.?value resource nic 'Microsoft.Network/networkInterfaces@2024-05-01' = { name: 'nic-workload-demo' location: location properties: { ipConfigurations: [ { name: 'primary' properties: { privateIPAllocationMethod: 'Dynamic' subnet: { id: resolvedSubnetId } } } ] } } The existing declaration only reads the network stack. It doesn’t redeploy it or take ownership of its resources. When no subnet parameter is supplied, the stack needs to exist and expose the subnetId output.
Use a Bicep version that supports @nullIfNotFound(); this example was compiled with Bicep 0.49.2. The decorator handles a resource that isn’t found, not missing read permissions. One source must supply a valid subnet ID. The final '' is only a fallback for a missing value, not a usable subnet; passing an empty string explicitly also overrides the stack output.
Here, the source stack lives at resource group scope. For a subscription-scoped stack that manages a resource group as described above, use scope: subscription() in the existing declaration instead. The output expression stays the same.
3. Deploy the workload stack az stack group create \ --name workload-demo \ --resource-group rg-workload-demo \ --template-file workload.bicep \ --action-on-unmanage detachAll \ --deny-settings-mode none To use a subnet supplied by the caller, add --parameters subnetId='<full-subnet-resource-id>' to that command. A non-null parameter overrides the stack output; leave it out to use the network stack.
The workload template uses the subnet without managing it or including a network module. All output lookup and consumption happens in Bicep; the CLI commands only submit the two stack deployments.
Where the deployment-time savings come from On the first rollout, the network stack must finish before the workload stack starts. For later changes:
Deploy the network stack when its template, parameters, or modules change. Let the workload’s Bicep template read the existing network stack’s outputs. Deploy only the workload stacks affected by the change. Run independent workload deployments in parallel where their dependencies allow it. You can read outputs from an unchanged source stack without redeploying it. Periodic drift checks and reconciliation still help catch changes made outside your templates.
Measure total pipeline time before and after the split. Slow resource providers, throttling, and additional stack calls can limit the savings.
Keeping within ARM’s 4 MB limit Microsoft documents a maximum of 4 MB per ARM template and 1 MB per resource definition. A parameter file is also limited to 4 MB. The template limits apply after expansion of iterative resource definitions and parameter and variable values. A deployment request can therefore be too large even when the source file is smaller than 4 MB.
Deploying the network and workloads separately keeps their infrastructure definitions out of the same request. Pass small outputs such as IDs instead of entire network objects or large configuration arrays.
When checking deployment sizes:
Every stack deployment must remain within the applicable ARM limits. Local Bicep modules improve structure but don’t guarantee a smaller main request. Linked templates offer different options from inline nested templates, but don’t remove all deployment limits. Check the generated ARM template and expansion during deployment, rather than relying on the size of the Bicep source file. Choosing your stack boundaries Group resources that change together and expose the values other stacks need. In this example, the workload can read the network stack’s output or use a subnet ID passed as a parameter.
Have the pipeline deploy only the affected stacks, then compare request sizes and pipeline timings with the original deployment. The split needs to reduce the work ARM handles on each run to be worth maintaining.
References Deployment stacks in Bicep ARM template best practices and limits Reference existing resources in Bicep The nullIfNotFound decorator Linked and nested templates Bicep outputs

content:
What is Cost allocation? In large enterprises, Azure services are often managed centrally but used by various departments. The central team usually wants to redistribute the cost of these shared services to the departments using them. This is where cost allocation in Azure’s Cost Management comes in.
Cost allocation allows you to reassign the costs of shared services from one subscription, resource group, or tag to another within your organization. It’s a way to shift the financial responsibility of shared services to the departments or business units that consume them, enhancing cost accountability.
However, it’s important to note that cost allocation doesn’t support purchases like reservations and savings plans. Also, it doesn’t affect your billing invoice or change billing responsibilities. Its primary function is to facilitate internal chargebacks, showing costs as they are reassigned or distributed.
The allocated costs are visible in cost analysis, appearing as other items associated with the targeted subscriptions, resource groups, or tags specified in your cost allocation rule.
Reference: Microsoft learn
How to Get Started with Cost Allocation? When it comes to cost allocation, the first step is deciding where your costs are coming from. You have three options to choose from:
Subscription Resource Group Tag Subscription/Resource Group When you choose either of these options, all the costs associated with the selected subscription or resource group will be taken into account. This includes the costs of all resources and services within the subscription or resource group.
Tags It’s important to note that if you choose Tags, some costs may still remain in the source subscription, like Defender for Cloud, even if you tag all the resources in a subscription. When tags are used, all the resources in your tenant with this tag will be selected.
Next, you’ll need to decide where these costs are going. Interestingly, you have the same three options as before. Allocating cost to a tag might seem a bit odd, and I haven’t tested this one yet, but it’s an option nonetheless.
Once you’ve selected your source and destination (targets), it’s time to decide how you want to distribute these costs. You have a few options here. You can choose to distribute the costs evenly or proportionally to:
Compute costs Network costs Storage costs Total costs Currently, there’s no API available to distribute costs proportionally, so you’ll need to configure this through the portal. If you’re planning to use the API for cost allocation, you’ll have to perform the calculations yourself. However, if you’re looking to distribute costs evenly, I’ve got you covered. I’ve written a handy PowerShell function to help with this.
function New-TargetResources { [CmdletBinding()] param ( [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipeline, ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName)] [string[]]$subscriptionId ) begin { $TargetResources $percentage = 100 / $subscriptionId.count } process { foreach ($subscription in $subscriptionId) { $TargetResources += @{ name = 'SubscriptionId' policyType = 'FixedProportion' resourceType = 'Dimension' values = @( @{ name = $subscription percentage = $percentage } ) } } } end { $TargetResources } } Practical Applications of Cost Allocation Case Study: Shared AKS Imagine you’re using a shared AKS cluster. You have multiple teams, each working on different node pools with different SKUs. In this scenario, you’d want to allocate the costs of each specific node pool to the appropriate team.
Step 1: Tagging the Node Pools The first step is to tag each node pool. This makes it clear which ’team’ it belongs to. In my case, I used a single tag that included an identifier of the workload and the environment, like this: wrkld-prod.
Step 2: Creating a Cost Allocation Rule Next, you’ll want to create a Cost Allocation Rule. Use the tag for the spoke as the source and distribute 100% to the corresponding subscription. The beauty of this is that the tag can now be used for other services as well. Simply tag the specific resource and it will automatically rearrange the costs to the subscription.
Case Study: Azure Firewall If you’re using a hub/spoke network model in Azure, chances are you have a central firewall in place where the traffic from your spoke is routed through. Cost allocation makes it possible to rearrange the cost from the subscription of the firewall to all the spokes.
Step 1: Retrieving All the Spokes First, you’ll need to retrieve all the spokes that you want to allocate the firewall cost to. I used the PowerShell cmdlet Get-AzManagementGroupSubscription to get all the subscription IDs.
Step 2: Creating the Target Objects You can use the PowerShell function above to distribute the costs evenly over all the subscriptions. If you want the costs to distribute proportionally to the network costs, you can do this step in the portal or retrieve information from the billing API.
Limitations to Keep in Mind There are a few limitations to keep in mind:
You cannot order the rules. The rules are executed in the order they were created. There is a function to allocate costs proportionally to network or compute cost, but this function is only available in the portal and not with the API. Target subscriptions are limited to 200. This means if you have a lot of spokes, you should consider only allocating to production subscriptions. You need to have EA administrator permissions, which you can’t give to an app registration. (I talked to microsoft and they are not implementing this any time soon) References Microsoft learn Rest API
